tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
I read the code for all three and tested your running MLX server. The first gap was described wrongly last session, the second has no principled reason behind it, and the third is real.

## 1. MLX and the reasoning setting

Your server does turn thinking off, so "the MLX server ignores the setting" was inaccurate. What actually happens:

- **The Rust client drops the setting.** `src/mlx/client.rs:105` takes `_reasoning` and sends `reasoning: None`.
- **The server has no such field.** `ChatCompletionRequest` in `mlx-server/schemas.py:67` only has model, messages, `max_tokens` and temperature.
- **The server turns thinking off itself, on every request.** `mlx-server/server.py:402` and `:437` pass `enable_thinking=False` to the chat template.

For your configured model this works. The `Qwen3.5-0.8B-OptiQ-4bit` template reads the flag and pre-fills an empty `<think></think>` block. I sent one test chat to `localhost:8678` with `max_tokens: 32`, and it answered in 3 tokens with `finish_reason: stop`.

The real gap is narrower:

- **The flag is only a template variable.** A model whose chat template never reads `enable_thinking` will think anyway, with no error. I could not check your commented-out `gemma-4-e4b-it-mxfp4`, because it is not in the local cache.
- **There is no fallback for that case.** The OpenRouter path retries with 2,048 extra tokens when a model refuses to stop reasoning (`src/app/dispatch.rs:882`). The MLX path has nothing equivalent.
- **The error would be misleading.** `server.py:419` counts completion tokens after stripping the thinking text. A model that spent its whole budget thinking reports `stop` with empty content, not `length`.

## 2. Why Jev is retried and chat is not

There is no design reason; the retry was added where failures were seen. HuggingFace is not a chat provider here: `src/huggingface/` only searches the Hub for models, so chat means MLX or OpenRouter.

- **Jev failed in live tests.** Commits `946366f` and `4e6944a` added the retry after a dropped connection hit one of three requests and left a cluster unlabelled.
- **Jev fans out.** `:topics` sends one Jev request per cluster, up to 8 at once, so rate limits and drops are much more likely than for the single chat request.
- **Chat already has a fallback when Jev is on.** A failed chat request falls back to the Jev taxonomy (`dispatch.rs:366`–`393`). Without `[jev]`, a chat failure goes straight to an error popup.
- **Neither chat client retries anything.** `OpenRouterClient::post` and `MlxClient` send once and set no timeout. This also covers embeddings.

Adding a retry to chat is reasonable, with two cautions:

- **OpenRouter:** a drop after generation means paying for the tokens twice.
- **MLX:** the server keeps generating after the client disconnects, on a single MLX thread. A retry queues behind the abandoned run.

I would retry connect and send errors plus 429/5xx, once or twice, in one helper shared by both clients.

## 3. Can the hint differ from what runs?

Yes. The hint comes from `topic_labeller_name()` (`dispatch.rs:617`), which looks only at config and is re-read on every frame (`src/ui/cluster.rs:266`). The route is decided later inside the spawned task.

With your config (`[jev]` with `propose_labels` on by default, plus MLX chat) the hint always says "MLX + Jev". What actually runs can be:

| What happens | Actual labeller |
|---|---|
| At least half the posts are in tech clusters and the proposal covers every cluster | MLX + Jev |

def generate(
    model: nn.Module,
    tokenizer: Union[PreTrainedTokenizer, TokenizerWrapper],
    prompt: Union[str, List[int]],
    verbose: bool = False,
    **kwargs,
) -> str:
    """

    Args:
       model (nn.Module): The language model.
       tokenizer (PreTrainedTokenizer): The tokenizer.
       prompt (Union[str, List[int]]): The input prompt string or integer tokens.

       kwargs: The remaining options get passed to :func:`stream_generate`.
          See :func:`stream_generate` for more details.
    """
    if verbose:
        print("=" * 10)

    text = ""
    for response in stream_generate(model, tokenizer, prompt, **kwargs):
        if verbose:
            print(response.text, end="", flush=True)
        text += response.text

    if verbose:

        print("=" * 10)
        if len(text) == 0:

        print(
            f"Generation: {response.generation_tokens} tokens, "
            f"{response.generation_tps:.3f} tokens-per-sec"
        )

    return text

    """Generate text using mlx-lm (text-only LLMs). Runs on the MLX thread."""
    from mlx_lm import stream_generate
    from mlx_lm.sample_utils import make_sampler

    prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        messages,
        tokenize=False,
        add_generation_prompt=True,
        enable_thinking=False,
    )
    sampler = make_sampler(temp=temp)
    generate_kwargs = {
        "prompt": prompt,
        "max_tokens": max_tokens,
        "sampler": sampler,
    }
    prompt_cache = _maybe_build_optiq_prompt_cache(model, model_id)
    if prompt_cache is not None:
        generate_kwargs["prompt_cache"] = prompt_cache

    # Streamed for its token counts and finish reason; `generate` returns
    # only the text.
    raw = ""
    last = None
    for last in cast(Any, stream_generate)(model, tokenizer, **generate_kwargs):
        raw += last.text

    if last is None:
        return ChatGeneration("", len(tokenizer.encode(prompt)), 0, 0, "stop")
    return _chat_generation(
        tokenizer, raw, last.prompt_tokens, last.generation_tokens, last.finish_reason
    )


def _generate_mlx_vlm(
    model, processor, messages: list[dict], max_tokens: int, temp: float
) -> ChatGeneration:
    """Generate text using mlx-vlm (vision-language models). Runs on the MLX thread."""
    from mlx_vlm import generate
    from mlx_vlm.prompt_utils import apply_chat_template

    prompt = cast(
        str,
        apply_chat_template(processor, model.config, messages, enable_thinking=False),
    )

    result = generate(
        model,
        processor,
        prompt,
        max_tokens=max_tokens,
        temperature=temp,
        enable_thinking=False,
    )

    return _chat_generation(
        getattr(processor, "tokenizer", processor),
        result.text,
        result.prompt_tokens,
        result.generation_tokens,
        getattr(result, "finish_reason", None),
        max_tokens,
    )


def _chat_generation(
    tokenizer,
    raw: str,
    prompt_tokens: int,
    generation_tokens: int,
    finish_reason: str | None,
    max_tokens: int | None = None,
) -> ChatGeneration:
    """Strip thinking from `raw` and account for the tokens it used.

    `enable_thinking=False` only works when the model's chat template reads
    it. A model that thinks anyway spends `max_tokens` on text that is
    stripped here, so the counts and finish reason come from what was
    generated, not from what is left.

    text = _strip_thinking(raw)
    if finish_reason is None:
        cut_off = max_tokens is not None and generation_tokens >= max_tokens
        finish_reason = "length" if cut_off else "stop"
    return ChatGeneration(
        text,
        prompt_tokens,
        generation_tokens,
        _reasoning_tokens(tokenizer, raw, text, generation_tokens),
        finish_reason,
    )


def _reasoning_tokens(tokenizer, raw: str, answer: str, generation_tokens: int) -> int:
    """Generated tokens that went to stripped thinking rather than the answer."""
    if answer == raw.strip():
        return 0
    answer_tokens = (
        len(tokenizer.encode(answer, add_special_tokens=False)) if answer else 0
    )
    return max(generation_tokens - answer_tokens, 1)

- With a `[jev]` config section and a chat model (MLX or a selected OpenRouter model), Jev first checks whether each cluster is about technology.
  - If at least half the posts are in tech clusters, the chat model proposes three candidate labels per cluster and Jev picks the best one for each cluster. No two clusters get the same label, and a cluster that none of the candidates fit shows as "Mixed".
  - Otherwise the chat model writes the labels itself, which works better on non-tech timelines.
  - Set `propose_labels = false` to skip the chat model.
- With `[jev]` and no chat model (or if the chat steps fail), Jev picks one topic per cluster from the fixed taxonomy. Clusters without a clear topic show as "Mixed". On a timeline dominated by one area, several clusters can land on the same broad topic; a finer `topics` list helps.
- Without `[jev]`, the chat model writes the labels.

Jev requests go out one per cluster, concurrently. Chat requests turn reasoning off so the short label budget isn't used up by hidden reasoning; models that require reasoning get low-effort reasoning and a larger budget instead.

new = old + "\nWhile labels are generated, the cluster list title names the labeller that is running at that moment (`generating labels via MLX + Jev...`). It names none during Jev's tech check, and it changes if the request falls back to another labeller.\n"
assert old in s; p.write_text(s.replace(old, new))

p = pathlib.Path("docs/jev-design.md"); s = p.read_text()
old = '''  that (Sonnet 5.5 returns 400 "Reasoning is mandatory") are retried with
  low-effort hidden reasoning and 2,048 extra tokens.
'''
new = old + '''- The MLX server takes no reasoning setting; it passes
  `enable_thinking=False` to the chat template on every request. That is a
  template variable, so a model whose template does not read it thinks
  anyway. The server now reports the generated token count, the real
  finish reason, and `usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`
  (tokens in the thinking it stripped). A reply that is cut off with
  reasoning tokens is requested once more with the same 2,048 extra tokens.
'''
assert old in s; p.write_text(s.replace(old, new))
EOF

old = "## Module Layout\n"
new = '''## Chat models

`ModelRegistry.get_chat_model` tries `mlx-lm` first and falls back to `mlx-vlm`. Thinking is always asked off: the server passes `enable_thinking=False` to the model's chat template and strips any thinking block from the answer. There is no request field for it.

`enable_thinking` is a template variable, so a model whose chat template does not read it thinks anyway, and that thinking uses `max_tokens`. The response says so:

- `usage.completion_tokens` counts every generated token, thinking included.
- `usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` counts the tokens in the thinking that was stripped.
- `finish_reason` is the backend's own (`length` when `max_tokens` ran out), even when nothing is left after stripping.

xplorertui asks once more with a larger `max_tokens` when a reply is cut off and has reasoning tokens.

## Module Layout
'''
assert s.count(old) == 1; p.write_text(s.replace(old, new))
EOF

content.text:
Both are done in the working tree, uncommitted, with no chat retries for dropped connections. Restart the server on port 8678 to pick up the budget change; it is still running the old code.

## Loading hint

The hint now shows the labeller that is actually running, not the one the config predicts.

- **How it works:** the `:topics` task sends a new `ClusterTopicsLabeller` event each time it starts a step that writes labels. The cluster list title reads that value.
- **What you see:** `generating labels...` during Jev's tech check, then `generating labels via MLX + Jev...` or `via MLX...`. If the request falls back to the taxonomy, it changes to `via Jev...`.
- **Removed:** `topic_labeller_name()`, the config-based guess.

## MLX budget headroom

Gemma is fine as configured: its chat template honours the thinking switch, and it answered the label prompt in 25 tokens on your running server. The fix covers models that think anyway.

- **Server reports what was generated.** `mlx-server/server.py` now returns the real generated-token count, the backend's own `finish_reason`, and `usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. Before, a reply that was all thinking came back as `stop` with empty content.
- **Client asks once more with room.** When an MLX reply is cut off and has reasoning tokens, `complete_text` in `src/app/dispatch.rs` repeats the request with 2,048 extra tokens, the same headroom the OpenRouter path uses. A reply cut off without reasoning is kept, since more room would not help.
- **Clearer error.** If the model is still thinking after the headroom, the popup says the budget was exhausted on reasoning.
- **One bug found on the way.** Some templates open the `<think>` block in the prompt, so the output only carries the closing tag. The server did not strip that, and the thinking leaked into the labels. It does now.

I forced thinking on with your two real models to check the accounting:

| Model | 48-token budget | With headroom |
|---|---|---|
| Gemma 4 e4b | cut off, empty answer | finished in 462 tokens, 27 of them the answer |
| Qwen3.5 0.8B | cut off, empty answer | still thinking at 2,096 tokens |

So headroom rescues a model that thinks briefly, not one that never stops. That case now gets the clear error.

## Verification

- **Rust:** 108 tests pass; `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy` are clean. New tests cover the headroom retry against a local stand-in server, and the hint state.
- **Server:** 46 pytest tests pass and ruff is clean. `ty` reports 3 findings, all in `image_security.py`, which I did not touch.
- **Live:** the modified server answered real requests on a spare port with the new usage fields.
- **Not run:** the hint through a real Jev request. The Jev URL is a constant, so only the chat-only route is tested end to end.

I also updated `README.md`, `docs/jev-design.md` and `mlx-server/AGENTS.md`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The server computed `finish_reason` from the text left after stripping. Deriving a status from cleaned output hides the very failure the status exists to report.
- `reasoning_tokens` under `completion_tokens_details` is the standard OpenAI usage field, so the client check is a single test that works for any provider reporting it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The retry rule is `reasoning_exhausted_budget()` in `src/openrouter/types.rs`: cut off and any reasoning tokens. Say if you want it stricter, for example only when the answer is empty.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ChatGeneration:
    """One chat reply, with thinking blocks already stripped from `text`."""

    text: str
    prompt_tokens: int
    # Every generated token, thinking included: this is what `max_tokens` caps.
    completion_tokens: int
    reasoning_tokens: int
    finish_reason: str


def _generate_mlx_lm(
    model,
    tokenizer,
    messages: list[dict],
    max_tokens: int,
    temp: float,
    model_id: str,
) -> ChatGeneration:
    """Generate text using mlx-lm (text-only LLMs). Runs on the MLX thread."""
    from mlx_lm import stream_generate
    from mlx_lm.sample_utils import make_sampler

    prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        messages,
        tokenize=False,
        add_generation_prompt=True,
        enable_thinking=False,
    )
    sampler = make_sampler(temp=temp)
    generate_kwargs = {
        "prompt": prompt,
        "max_tokens": max_tokens,
        "sampler": sampler,
    }
    prompt_cache = _maybe_build_optiq_prompt_cache(model, model_id)
    if prompt_cache is not None:
        generate_kwargs["prompt_cache"] = prompt_cache

    # Streamed for its token counts and finish reason; `generate` returns
    # only the text.
    raw = ""
    last = None
    for last in cast(Any, stream_generate)(model, tokenizer, **generate_kwargs):
        raw += last.text

    if last is None:
        return ChatGeneration("", len(tokenizer.encode(prompt)), 0, 0, "stop")
    return _chat_generation(
        tokenizer,
        _reopen_thinking(prompt, raw),
        last.prompt_tokens,
        last.generation_tokens,
        last.finish_reason,
    )


def _generate_mlx_vlm(
    model, processor, messages: list[dict], max_tokens: int, temp: float
) -> ChatGeneration:
    """Generate text using mlx-vlm (vision-language models). Runs on the MLX thread."""
    from mlx_vlm import generate
    from mlx_vlm.prompt_utils import apply_chat_template

    prompt = cast(
        str,
        apply_chat_template(processor, model.config, messages, enable_thinking=False),
    )

    result = generate(
        model,
        processor,
        prompt,
        max_tokens=max_tokens,
        temperature=temp,
        enable_thinking=False,
    )

    return _chat_generation(
        getattr(processor, "tokenizer", processor),
        _reopen_thinking(prompt, result.text),
        result.prompt_tokens,
        result.generation_tokens,
        getattr(result, "finish_reason", None),
        max_tokens,
    )


def _chat_generation(
    tokenizer,
    raw: str,
    prompt_tokens: int,
    generation_tokens: int,
    finish_reason: str | None,
    max_tokens: int | None = None,
) -> ChatGeneration:
    """Strip thinking from `raw` and account for the tokens it used.

    `enable_thinking=False` only works when the model's chat template reads
    it. A model that thinks anyway spends `max_tokens` on text that is
    stripped here, so the counts and finish reason come from what was
    generated, not from what is left.
    """
    text = _strip_thinking(raw)
    if finish_reason is None:
        cut_off = max_tokens is not None and generation_tokens >= max_tokens
        finish_reason = "length" if cut_off else "stop"
    return ChatGeneration(
        text,
        prompt_tokens,
        generation_tokens,
        _reasoning_tokens(tokenizer, raw, text, generation_tokens),
        finish_reason,
    )


def _reopen_thinking(prompt: str, raw: str) -> str:
    """Restore a `<think>` tag that the chat template put in the prompt.

    Some templates end the prompt with an open thinking block, so the model's
    output starts inside it and carries only the closing tag.
    """
    if prompt.rstrip().endswith("<think>"):
        return "<think>" + raw
    return raw


def _reasoning_tokens(tokenizer, raw: str, answer: str, generation_tokens: int) -> int:
    """Generated tokens that went to stripped thinking rather than the answer."""
    if answer == raw.strip():
        return 0
    answer_tokens = (
        len(tokenizer.encode(answer, add_special_tokens=False)) if answer else 0
    )
    return max(generation_tokens - answer_tokens, 1)



def _strip_thinking(text: str) -> str:
    """Remove reasoning/thinking blocks from generated text.

    Handles multiple formats:
    - <think>...</think> (Qwen, DeepSeek)
    - <channel|>...<|channel> and <|channel>...<channel|> (Gemma 4)
    """
    import re

    # <think>...</think> — greedy within blocks, DOTALL for multiline
    text = re.sub(r"<think>.*?</think>", "", text, flags=re.DOTALL)
    # Unclosed <think> at the start — strip everything from <think> onward
    if "<think>" in text:
        text = text[: text.index("<think>")]
    text = _strip_gemma_channel_blocks(text)
    return text.strip()

git add -A README.md docs mlx-server src && git status --short && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Show the running labeller in the :topics hint; give MLX thinking its own budget

The loading hint named the labeller the config predicted ("MLX + Jev"),
but the route is chosen at run time: a non-tech timeline uses the chat
model alone, and a failed or partial proposal falls back to the Jev
taxonomy. The :topics task now sends `ClusterTopicsLabeller` when it
starts a step that writes labels, and the cluster list title shows that.
It names no labeller during Jev's tech check.

The MLX server passes `enable_thinking=False` to the chat template, but
that is a template variable: a model whose template does not read it
thinks anyway and spent the 32-256 token label budget on text that is
stripped. On the server, `max_tokens` now caps the answer only. Thinking
gets up to 2,048 extra tokens in the same run, so the client sends one
request. The server streams the generation to do this, and now reports
the backend's finish reason, the full generated token count and
`usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. It used to derive
the finish reason from the stripped text, so a reply that was all
thinking came back as "stop" with empty content.

Also strip thinking when the template opens the `<think>` block in the
prompt, so the output has only the closing tag. That thinking used to
leak into the labels.

An MLX reply that is still all thinking after the headroom now reports
that the budget was exhausted, not just "empty content".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

gh pr create --base main --title "Show the running labeller in the :topics hint; give MLX thinking its own budget" --body-file - <<'EOF'
Two follow-ups to #93. Chat requests are still sent once; there is no retry for dropped connections and no second request for budget.

## Loading hint

The hint named the labeller the config predicted (`MLX + Jev`), but the route is chosen at run time from Jev's tech check and can fall back.

- The `:topics` task sends a new `ClusterTopicsLabeller` event when it starts a step that writes labels.
- The cluster list title shows that value: `generating labels...` during the tech check, then `via MLX + Jev...` or `via MLX...`, and `via Jev...` if it falls back to the taxonomy.
- `topic_labeller_name()`, the config-based guess, is removed.

## MLX thinking budget

The MLX server passes `enable_thinking=False` to the chat template. That is a template variable, so a model whose template does not read it thinks anyway and spent the 32–256 token label budget on text that is stripped.

- On the server, `max_tokens` now caps the answer only. Thinking gets up to 2,048 extra tokens (`THINKING_HEADROOM_TOKENS`) in the same run. A model that does not think stops at `max_tokens` as before.
- The server streams the generation to do this (`mlx_lm.stream_generate` / `mlx_vlm.stream_generate`).
- The response reports the backend's finish reason, the full generated token count and `usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. The finish reason used to be derived from the stripped text, so a reply that was all thinking came back as `stop` with empty content.
- Thinking is also stripped when the template opens the `<think>` block in the prompt and the output has only the closing tag. That used to leak into the labels.
- An MLX reply that is still all thinking after the headroom reports "exhausted token budget", not "empty content".

## Testing

- `cargo test --locked --all-features --all-targets`: 105 passed. `cargo fmt -- --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets` are clean.
- `uv run pytest -q` in `mlx-server`: 44 passed. `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are clean. `ty check` reports 3 findings in `image_security.py`, which this PR does not touch.
- Real models, with the template made to ignore the flag and a 48-token budget: Gemma 4 e4b thought for 384–523 tokens and returned the complete labels in one run with `finish_reason: stop`. Qwen3.5 0.8B never stopped thinking and returned `length` with empty content after the headroom.
- Both models with the flag honoured, through `mlx-lm` and `mlx-vlm`: same output as before, cut at `max_tokens` when the answer is long.
- Not tested: the hint through a real Jev request (the Jev URL is a constant). The chat-only route is tested end to end against a local stand-in server.

A running MLX server needs a restart to pick this up.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

content.text:
I read "once this is resolved" as: no second chat request. The budget fix now lives on the server in a single run, and the PR is open: https://github.com/jessearmand/xplorertui/pull/94

## What changed since the last summary

- **No second request.** The client-side repeat with 2,048 extra tokens is gone. The Rust MLX path sends one request, as before.
- **The server gives thinking its own room.** `max_tokens` now caps the answer only. Thinking that a model does anyway gets up to 2,048 extra tokens in the same run. A model that does not think stops at `max_tokens` exactly as before.
- **Streaming on both backends.** The server now streams the generation to count answer and thinking tokens as they arrive, for `mlx-lm` and `mlx-vlm`.

The loading hint change is as described earlier, unchanged.

## Verification

- **Gemma, forced to think, 48-token budget:** three runs thought for 384–523 tokens and each returned the complete labels in one run.
- **Small Qwen, forced to think:** never stopped thinking; it returns empty content with `finish_reason: length` after the headroom, and the app shows the "exhausted token budget" error.
- **Both models as configured:** same output as before through both backends, cut at `max_tokens` when the answer is long.
- **Suites:** 105 Rust tests and 44 server tests pass; `cargo fmt`, `clippy` and `ruff` are clean. `ty` still reports 3 findings in `image_security.py`, which the PR does not touch.
- **Not run:** the hint through a real Jev request.

## Things to know

- **Restart the server on port 8678.** It is still running the old code.
- **One commit.** Both changes touch `src/app/dispatch.rs`, so I did not split them. The branch is `topics-hint-and-mlx-thinking-headroom`.
- **`completion_tokens` can now exceed `max_tokens`** in the server's response, because it counts thinking too.
- **Bend:** there is no `PROOF.bend` in the repo, so that pre-commit step did not apply.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Putting the headroom on the server means the wasted first run disappears: a thinking model costs its thinking once, not a discarded run plus a full rerun.
- My first forced-thinking probe wrapped the tokenizer, which silently dropped Gemma's end-of-turn stop token and made answers run long. Patching the template on the real tokenizer object fixed the probe; the server code was not affected.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Here is a note offered by a side agent:

> Heads up · The one-run fix changes what `max_tokens` means on your MLX server, so a model that never stops thinking can run far longer.
>
> **MLX `max_tokens` now caps only the answer**
> The main agent is replacing the second request with a single run on the server (`mlx-server/server.py`).
> * **Before:** `max_tokens` capped everything the model generated, thinking included.
> * **Now:** it caps only the answer. Thinking gets up to **2,048 extra tokens** in the same run (`THINKING_HEADROOM_TOKENS`).
> * **Unaffected:** models that switch thinking off, like your Gemma and small Qwen. They stop at the same point as before.
> * **Cost:** a model that never stops thinking now runs to the full cap before failing. In the forced test, the small Qwen did exactly that.
> * **Side effect:** any other client of this server gets the new meaning too.
> **Restart the server on port 8678** to pick this up.

Track thinking per token without rescanning the reply

`_collect_reply` stripped the whole reply so far after every token to
tell thinking from answer. That work grows with the square of the reply
length, and it runs on the single MLX thread, so one request with a very
large `max_tokens` could hold the server for a long time.

A small tracker now looks only at the new segment plus the few carried
characters that could start a tag. The reply is stripped once, at the
end.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text:
A background security review flagged a resource-exhaustion problem in `mlx-server/server.py`. I fixed the one my commit introduced, pushed it to PR #94, and restarted the server on port 8678 with the fix.

The notification gave only the category, not the details, so this is the issue I found under that heading:

- **The problem:** to tell thinking from answer, the server re-stripped the whole reply so far after every token. That work grows with the square of the reply length, and it runs on the single MLX thread. One request with a very large `max_tokens` could hold the server for a long time.
- **The fix:** a small tracker now looks only at the new token plus the few carried characters that could start a tag. The reply is stripped once, at the end.
- **Checked:** 46 server tests pass, including one for tags split across tokens and one that the carried text stays shorter than a tag. On real Gemma runs forced to think, the counts match the earlier ones (about 500 thinking tokens, complete labels, one run).

One related thing I left alone: the server accepts any `max_tokens` value from a request, with no upper limit. That was already the case before this PR, and the server only listens on localhost. A cap would be a one-line change in `mlx-server/schemas.py`; say if you want one and what limit.

The server is running as a background task of this session again, with the log at `scratchpad/mlx-server.log`. Two earlier background starts show as failed: one is the old server I stopped, and one failed on a relative log path before starting anything.

content.text:
The PR had one review comment, from Codex, and it is fixed, answered and resolved on [PR #94](https://github.com/jessearmand/xplorertui/pull/94). CI on the new commit was still running when I checked; `fmt` and GitGuardian had passed and the rest were pending.

## The comment

When the server stopped a reply at the answer cap, it closed the model's token stream early. The stream's detokenizer can hold back the text of the newest tokens until a later token arrives, so that text was lost even though its tokens were counted.

The reviewer was right, and I reproduced it on a real model: through `mlx-vlm`, Gemma with a 6-token cap returned "Cluster 0: Rust" when the tokens spelled "Cluster 0: Rust programming".

## The fix

- **What changed:** when the server stops a reply itself, it now rebuilds the text from the generated tokens with a fresh detokenizer of the same kind the stream uses. A reply that ends on its own is handled as before.
- **Why not finalize the stream's own detokenizer:** neither library exposes it. `mlx-lm` hands out a new instance on each access, and `mlx-vlm` makes a private copy.
- **Tests:** the test stream now behaves like the real `mlx-lm` one, and three new tests cover held-back text at the cap, with and without thinking. 49 server tests pass; ruff is clean.
- **Real models:** the 6-token Gemma case now returns "Cluster 0: Rust programming" through both backends, and the forced-thinking runs still return complete labels in one run.

The commit is `1f515e7` in `mlx-server/server.py` and `mlx-server/test_chat_usage.py`. No Rust code changed.

## Server

I restarted the server on port 8678 with this fix; it returns the full 6-token text over HTTP. It still runs as a background task of this session, logging to `scratchpad/mlx-server.log`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Streamed text and generated tokens are not the same sequence. A streaming detokenizer emits text only when it is sure of it, so stopping a stream by closing it can drop the last word.
- My first test stream sent each token's text immediately, so it could not show this bug. Making the fake mirror the real stream's shape is what let the tests catch it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

     segments: list[str] = []
     tokens: list[Any] = []
     prompt_tokens = generated = reasoning_tokens = 0
+    # Tokens whose text may be the start of a thinking tag split across

+    pending = 0

+                pending = 0
+            elif thinking.partial_tag:
+                pending += step

         self._carry = text[pos:][-(_LONGEST_THINKING_TAG - 1) :]
         return thinking
 
+    @property
+    def partial_tag(self) -> bool:
+        """True if the stream, outside a thinking block, ends with the start
+        of an opening tag (e.g. `<th`), so its last tokens can't be classified
+        yet."""
+        if self._closing_tag is not None:
+            return False
+        return any(
+            self._carry.endswith(tag[:n])
+            for tag in _THINKING_TAGS
+            for n in range(1, len(tag))
+        )
+
 
 def _maybe_build_optiq_prompt_cache(model, model_id: str):

index 86d32a3..f33a6c8 100644
--- a/mlx-server/test_chat_usage.py
+++ b/mlx-server/test_chat_usage.py

     result = chat(segments)
     assert result["content"] == "Rust tooling"
     assert result["finish_reason"] == "stop"
-    # The first fragment cannot be told from answer text yet.
+    # The first fragment is held back, then counted as thinking.
+    assert result["reasoning_tokens"] == 5
+
+
+def test_split_opening_tag_does_not_use_the_answer_budget(chat):
+    # MAX_TOKENS is 4: charging `<th` to the answer would cut "d".
+    segments = ["<th", "ink>", "hm", "</think>", "a ", "b ", "c ", "d"]
+    result = chat(segments)
+    assert result["content"] == "a b c d"
     assert result["reasoning_tokens"] == 4
 
 
+def test_split_closing_tag_with_thinking_opened_by_the_prompt(chat):
+    segments = ["hm", "</th", "ink>", "a ", "b ", "c ", "d"]
+    result = chat(segments, prompt_suffix="\nassistant: <think>\n")
+    assert result["content"] == "a b c d"
+    assert result["reasoning_tokens"] == 3
+
+
+def test_text_that_only_looks_like_a_tag_start_is_answer(chat):
+    result = chat(["a ", "<", "b ", "c ", "d ", "e"])

+    assert result["finish_reason"] == "length"
+    assert result["reasoning_tokens"] == 0
+
+
 def test_tracking_work_does_not_grow_with_the_reply():

cd /Users/jessearmand/Develop/xdevplatform/xplorertui && git add mlx-server/server.py mlx-server/test_chat_usage.py && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Hold tokens that may start a thinking tag until the tag is known

When an opening tag is split across tokens (`<th`, `ink>`), the first
fragment was counted as answer before the tag was recognised. It used
answer budget, was left out of `reasoning_tokens`, and with a small
`max_tokens` the reply could stop on the fragment and return it.

Tokens whose text ends with the start of an opening tag are now held:
they count as thinking if the tag completes and as answer if it does
not. Held tokens that turn out to be answer are all counted at once, so
the reply is trimmed back to `max_tokens` when they pass it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push 2>&1 | tail -1; git log --oneline -1; gh api repos/jessearmand/xplorertui/pulls/94/comments/4242545561/replies -f body='Fixed in the latest commit. Tokens whose text ends with the start of an opening tag are now held: they count as thinking if the tag completes and as answer if it does not. `<th` + `ink>` is counted as two thinking tokens, and with `max_tokens = 1` the reply no longer stops on the fragment.

One consequence handled as well: held tokens that turn out to be answer text are all counted at once, which could take the answer a few tokens past `max_tokens` (`a b c < t h x` with a cap of 4 returned 7 tokens). The reply is now trimmed back to the cap in that case.

Tests cover a split opening tag against the answer budget, a split closing tag when the prompt opened the block, text that only looks like a tag start, and the trim.' --jq '.html_url'; gh api graphql -f query='mutation { resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:"PRRT_kwDORSGDdM6rP4-y"}) { thread { isResolved } } }' --jq '.data.resolveReviewThread.thread.isResolved'; lsof -iTCP:8678 -sTCP:LISTEN -P -n | tail -1; pgrep -fl "uvicorn server:app" | cut -c1-40; git status --short

content.text:
The one open review comment on [PR #94](https://github.com/jessearmand/xplorertui/pull/94) is fixed, answered and resolved, and the local changes turned out to be a fix for that same comment. CI on the new commit (`43d7ab8`) was still running when I checked.

## The local changes

- **What was there:** uncommitted edits to `mlx-server/server.py` and `mlx-server/test_chat_usage.py`, plus an untracked `xplorertui-pr94-fix.diff`. The diff file is an exact copy of those edits.
- **What they do:** they address the Codex comment about thinking tags split across tokens. A token whose text ends with the start of an opening tag (`<th`) is held, then counted as thinking if the tag completes or as answer if it does not.
- **Verdict:** the approach is sound and its tests pass, so I kept it. I found one gap and fixed it.

## The gap

When held tokens turn out to be answer text, they are all counted at once, so the answer could run past `max_tokens`. With a cap of 4, the tokens `a b c < t h x` came back as 7 tokens. The reply is now trimmed back to the cap in that case, with a test for it.

## Verification

- 53 server tests pass; ruff is clean. `ty` still reports the same 3 findings in `image_security.py`.
- Real Gemma runs behave as before: complete labels in one run when forced to think, and the 6-token cap returns the full six tokens' text.

## Housekeeping

- **`xplorertui-pr94-fix.diff`:** I left it untracked in the repo root and did not commit it. Its content is now in the commit, so it can be deleted.
- **Server:** I restarted the one on port 8678 with the fix. It is still this session's background task, logging to `scratchpad/mlx-server.log`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Deferring a decision has a cost at the moment it resolves. Holding tokens fixed the misclassification, but releasing several at once is what let the answer overshoot the cap.
- The trim is safe only because the released tokens are the last ones generated and all of them are answer, so dropping from the tail removes exactly the excess.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
